To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the lifetime trend of urinary Cd (U‐Cd) is nonlinear and nonmononotonic and is driven mainly by recent intake of Cd and variations in urinary excretion of creatine and proteins, which are unrelated to metal accumulation or toxicity.
the relationship of U-Cd and U-Cr with age was not monotonic and was driven by physiological variations in the urinary excretion of creatine and proteins.

1) urinary Cd (U–Cd) is not a reliable biomarker for the Cd body burden at low Cd exposure levels; 2) U–Cd is associated with age in both genders through nonlinear and non-monotonic relationships, which appear to be driven primarily by recent Cd intake; 3) these relationships are amplified by the coexcretion with proteins; 4) the U–Cd level in smokers is not associated with the duration of exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of exposure to environmental pollutants and occupational exposures on human health.
the effects of cadmium exposure on human health, with special emphasis on kidney function.
the study of the relationships between urinary cadmium and age and urinary proteins, and the influence of these relationships on the interpretation of the results of biomonitoring studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
U-Cd levels are associated with age in a nonlinear and nonmonotonous manner.

urinary Cd levels in the general population of adults and adolescents are influenced by a variety of factors including gender, diuresis, and protein tubule reabsorption, and these factors are more important than age in explaining urinary Cd levels.
urinary Cd is not a reliable biomarker to assess Cd body burden in the general population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the urinary Cd concentration in adults and elderly people is not a reliable biomarker for Cd body burden.
the urinary Cd concentration is not a reliable indicator of the total Cd burden.
Cd exposure and accumulation in humans, and the resulting health effects, are not well characterized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the urinary cadmium (U-Cd)/creatinine ratio is not a good biomarker of the cadmium body burden in humans.
urinary cadmium (U-Cd), the biomarker used to assess Cd body burden, does not increase linearly with age.

urinary Cd is not a reliable biomarker at the population level because of its large variability, which is unrelated to the body burden and is mainly driven by physiological changes in the excretion and reabsorption of proteins.
